clue.text: Poet's residence by river

parts.note: a residence is where you live, your home

explanation.surface: Describes a poet's house standing beside a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after Poet is a link ('Poet is ...'), not a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek author of the Iliad and the Odyssey is the archetypal epic poet.

clue.text: Bad smell linked to papa? It's a hunch

parts.note: a hum is British slang for an unpleasant smell
Papa is P in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone suspects a nasty smell is connected to their father.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hunch' looks like a suspicion, as the surface suggests; here it means a lump on the back.
explanation.definitionFit: A hunch is a bump or protuberance, such as on a hunchback, which is another word for a hump.

clue.text: Fix blokes drinks at the outset…

parts.note: blokes is British slang for men

indicators.note: at the outset points to the opening letter of the word drinks

explanation.surface: An instruction to sort out the men's drinks before anything else.
explanation.definitionFit: To fix something broken is to repair it, a direct synonym.

clue.text: … A justification to share out beer?

parts.note: to ration supplies is to share them out in fixed amounts
ale is a type of beer

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: asks what excuse there could be for dividing up the beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A rationale is the underlying reasoning that serves as a justification for something.

clue.text: Drifting wreckage seen as half of family lost at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused or disordered, so the pooled letters are jumbled together
half of takes the first three of the six letters of family

explanation.surface: Wreckage floating about is seen as half of a family drowned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost at sea' reads as drowning, but 'lost' is fodder and 'at sea' alone signals the anagram, which covers FAM as well.
explanation.definitionFit: Flotsam is the floating debris of a wrecked ship or its cargo.

clue.text: Discussion groups university introduced to classes

indicators.note: introduced to says one piece is put into the middle of the other

parts.note: in British schools a class or year group is called a form

explanation.surface: Debating societies brought into the university's classes.
explanation.definitionFit: Forums are meetings or online spaces where people gather to discuss topics.

clue.text: Former heads of our legal department

indicators.note: heads of takes the leading letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: Refers to the people who used to run our legal department.
explanation.definitionFit: Old can mean previous, as in an old boss, meaning a former one.

clue.text: Fruity buns turn scorched on the outside?

indicators.note: fruity suggests something mixed up and colourful, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Fruit buns that turn burnt on the outside in the oven.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin burnt by the sun is scorched on the surface of the body, the question mark flagging the playful phrasing.

clue.text: Contemplate friend consuming awful diet

indicators.note: consuming means swallowing up, so one piece takes the other inside it

parts.note: a mate is a friend in British usage

indicators.note: awful suggests something messed up, so the letters of diet are rearranged

explanation.surface: A friend eats a terrible diet while thinking things over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' rearranges the fodder to EDIT before it goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To contemplate is to think deeply or reflect, the same as to meditate.

clue.text: Cleric leaving one place of worship

indicators.note: leaving says a piece departs from the longer word

parts.note: a minister is a cleric of a church
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A clergyman quits his church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleric' looks like the definition but is the fodder; the definition is at the other end.
explanation.definitionFit: A minster is a large church, such as York Minster, a place of worship.

clue.text: Ate some shortbread in Edinburgh

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone had a little shortbread while visiting the Scottish capital.
explanation.definitionFit: To have eaten a meal is to have had dinner, the past tense matching Ate.

clue.text: Comedian keeping end of jokes clean is matter of space

indicators.note: keeping means holding inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a comic is a comedian

indicators.note: end of takes the final letter of the word jokes

parts.note: to dust is to clean surfaces

explanation.surface: A comedian keeping his act free of smut, that is the matter at hand.
explanation.definitionFit: The fine particles drifting between stars and planets are interstellar matter found in outer space.

clue.text: Bridge news: a much-loved part of The Times

definitions.text: a much-loved part of The Times

parts.note: to bridge a gap is to cross it
word means news, as in 'any word from him?'

explanation.surface: A headline about the card game bridge, in a much-loved newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge news' suggests the card game column; Bridge is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: The daily puzzle the solver is doing right now is one of the newspaper's best-loved features.

clue.text: Wear thin, possibly becoming bare

indicators.note: possibly says these letters could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Clothes that wear thin may leave you exposed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone naked is said to be undressed in this idiom, so the phrase means without clothes.

clue.text: Game in which St Helens initially defend after turnover

indicators.note: after turnover says the whole assembled string is then flipped end to end
initially takes the opening letter of Helens

parts.note: to guard is to defend

explanation.surface: A rugby league match where St Helens defends after losing possession.
explanation.walkthrough: St Helens is a rugby league club; a turnover is losing the ball. ST, H and GUARD are reversed as one string.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the British name for the board game Americans call checkers.

clue.text: Definitely not embracing king and country

indicators.note: embracing means hugging, so one piece takes the other inside it

parts.note: no way is an emphatic refusal, definitely not
R is the abbreviation for king, from Latin rex

explanation.surface: A firm refusal to embrace both monarch and nation.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scandinavian kingdom, so it is an example of a country.

clue.text: New throne for queen, perhaps

indicators.note: new says the letters are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A new throne for the queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'queen' suggests royalty, matching throne, but the queen here is an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: Colonies of these large wasps are founded by a queen, so a queen is one example.

clue.text: Fight Club follows The Big Sleep (final cut)

indicators.note: follows puts the club after the other piece
final cut says the last letter is removed

parts.note: the Big Sleep, the title of a famous film, is read as a long unconscious state, a coma
a bat is a club used in games such as cricket

explanation.surface: The film Fight Club is ranked after The Big Sleep, in its director's cut.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as two film titles and a film term; each is used for its plain words.
explanation.definitionFit: Combat is fighting, especially between armed forces, a synonym for fight.

clue.text: Rhyming couplet that has four sprightly feet?

definitions.text: Rhyming couplet that has four sprightly feet?

parts.words: Rhyming couplet that has four sprightly feet?
parts.note: the two words of the answer rhyme, making a couplet, and the small creature it names scurries on four nimble feet, not metrical ones

explanation.surface: Reads like a definition from verse, a couplet with four metrical feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feet' and 'couplet' suggest poetic metre, but the feet belong to a small animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The common rodent that lives in homes is a pair of rhyming words and runs on four quick feet.

clue.text: Cambridge boat's gamble

definitions.meaning: a flat-bottomed boat pushed with a pole, famously used on the river Cam in Cambridge
in British English, to have a ... is to place a bet or take a chance

explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the pole-driven boat seen in Cambridge and, informally, a bet.

clue.text: Mop of hair caught up in extractor fan

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the letters read from bottom to top
caught says letters are trapped within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A head of hair gets sucked into a kitchen extractor fan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught' finds ORFA across 'extractor fan'; 'up' reverses it in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A rounded bushy hairstyle of tightly curled hair is a mop of hair.

clue.text: Book a woman's back treatment

indicators.note: back says the assembled letters are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: her is the possessive meaning a woman's

explanation.surface: Booking a woman in for back treatment.
explanation.definitionFit: Rehab is short for rehabilitation, a course of treatment, especially for addiction.

clue.text: Expression of dissent forbidden? No thanks!

indicators.note: no says the following piece is absent from the longer word

parts.note: something taboo is forbidden
ta is informal British for thanks

explanation.surface: Refusing a forbidden offer with a polite no thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: A jeer from an audience shows disapproval, which is an expression of dissent.

clue.text: Bard's beginning revision of woeful epic poem

indicators.note: beginning takes the opening letter of the word Bard's
revision of means a reworking, so the letters of woeful are rearranged

explanation.surface: A poet's opening redraft of a terrible epic.
explanation.definitionFit: An Old English saga about a hero who slays Grendel, the best-known early epic poem in English.

clue.text: A loud cry after wife's total failure

indicators.note: after puts the clue's first pieces behind the wife's letter

parts.note: W is an abbreviation for wife
a shout is a loud cry

explanation.surface: A man's yell after his wife's complete disaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A complete flop, especially an event rained off or a hopeless person, is a total failure.

clue.text: The same detective returned over the top

parts.note: DI is a Detective Inspector

indicators.note: returned says the letters are turned to run backwards

parts.note: OTT is the abbreviation for over the top, meaning excessive

explanation.surface: The same detective came back, and went too far.
explanation.definitionFit: Ditto is used to say what was just said applies again, meaning likewise.
